name: Hokitika Airfield
before:
The West Coast's air link, just under 2 km from Hokitika and the nearest scheduled airport to Greymouth, 40 km up the coast and the largest settlement on that side of the island. For a South Island itinerary taking in the glaciers it saves a long drive across the island.

It is small and honest about it: one terminal, two tarmac gates, and aircraft up to ATR 72 size flown by Air New Zealand. There are car hire desks and a cafe, which is the whole of it. Two sealed runways cross the site, the longer at 1,152 metres.

The aerodrome is uncontrolled and owned by the local district council through Destination Westland.

It has a good claim to being where scheduled flying in New Zealand started. Air Travel (NZ) Ltd, founded by Bert Mercer in 1934, flew the country's first scheduled service from here to Haast on 18 December 1934.
after:
Hokitika's airport, which also serves Greymouth, up the coast to the north. According to the Department of Conservation it is the closest commercial airport to Westland Tai Poutini National Park, home of the Franz Josef and Fox glaciers, so for a glacier itinerary it saves a long drive across the island.

It is small and honest about it: one terminal and daily Air New Zealand flights to Christchurch. There are car hire desks and a cafe, which is the whole of it.

Destination Westland, a company controlled by Westland District Council, runs the airport.

claims.why: Wrong on Wikipedia's own figures: runway 03/21 is 1,152 m but 12/30 is 1,176 m. OurAirports gives 03/21 as 1,314 m, which is Wikipedia's 1,152 m plus its 81 m starter extension at each end. The AIP chart could not be read: the plain fetch returned an empty page and the browser was sent on to a plain-HTTP address, which the session's proxy refuses. That both runways are sealed is confirmed (OurAirports lists 03/21 and 12/30 as asphalt; Wikipedia says two sealed runways) but is left out for length.

claims.claim: the country's first scheduled service, from here to Haast, on 18 December 1934
claims.wasBefore: It has a good claim to being where scheduled flying in New Zealand started. Air Travel (NZ) Ltd, founded by Bert Mercer in 1934, flew the country's first scheduled service from here to Haast on 18 December 1934.
claims.why: Good sources disagree on the destination: Wikipedia says the first flight went from Hokitika to Haast, but the aviation history blog, quoting the Christchurch Press, has the inaugural service on 18 December 1934 flying Inchbonnie, Hokitika and Franz Josef, with the Hokitika to Haast mail service starting on 31 December. 'From here' was wrong: the company flew from the old Southside aerodrome, and today's airport opened in 1951. Rewritten to what both sources support (see above).

claims.claim: terminal opening hours; the drive to the national park
claims.why: Held back: new, and each on one organisation's word. The airport's site gives terminal opening hours of 8am to 10am and 4pm to 6pm on weekdays, 8am to 10am on Saturdays and 4pm to 6pm on Sundays (so the building opens around the flights), and the Department of Conservation puts Westland Tai Poutini National Park about an hour and a half's drive south of Hokitika.

claims.claim: the Air Travel (NZ) history: first airline, Bert Mercer, services from 18 December 1934, the older aerodrome, today's airport of 1951
claims.wasBefore: It has a good claim to being where scheduled flying in New Zealand started.
claims.why: Held back for Andy (cut in review, 23 Sep): the helper's corrected history rests on Wikipedia and the 3rd Level New Zealand aviation history blog, which quotes the Christchurch Press of 1934. The brief takes blogs only as a last-resort tie-breaker, and Te Ara and NZHistory refused (403). It also shows the old text was wrong twice: the 1934 flights used the older Southside aerodrome (today's Seaview airport opened in 1951), and the sources disagree on where the first service went. Could come back with Te Ara, NZHistory or a museum as the second source.
